- Good evening, Dr. McDade and school board members. My name is Dr. Yibo Zhang, my address is on file. After serving on the superintendent's advisory council of equity for two years, I would like to share some of my insights from this journey.

First of all, what does equity actually mean? To me, the answer to this question started to form a long time ago. My dad was born in an extremely impoverished village. For generations, he was the only one who admitted to a four-year college.

After well-established with a job, he continued to give back to his rural community while raising up our own family. His actions planted a seed in my heart of equity, though at that time, I had no idea what equity actually meant.

I even sometimes saw his actions as irrelevant to my own educational worlds. As I grow, I learned that fitting various individual needs into the bigger picture of societal needs is a challenging work, and reconciling all of them is a challenging work that we call equity.

I learned that there is no single definition of equity, as equity is context dependent. Equity conversations, PD sessions are important, especially at the beginning of this work. But what becomes truly impactful is equity become the backdrop and mindset for our work that we do.

Just like I explained to my kids, I say I love you, that's the backdrop of our family and directs all we do on a daily basis. It does not make sense I say I'm too busy to love you. In the same way, equity is not some actual work, but our work that we do.

Next, I would like to use this graph to illustrate what equity look like when we quantify it. Every single student should move to their next level of development by effective program factors, regardless of their ethnicity, learning disability, English proficiency level.

What matters should be our program factors. By that, I mean we should have one or multiple programs that help students get to where they need to be. Equity is not another meeting. Let's make it-- Thank you. I'll work with you. Thank you.
